item.title: Statistics: Benford's Law — Daily Learning
item.description: In many real-world datasets, 1 is the leading digit about 30% of the time and 9 only about 5%, far from the roughly 11% each you would expect if digits were random. That uneven falloff is a tripwire for made-up numbers.

item.title: Big Idea: The Sleeping Beauty Problem — Daily Learning
item.description: On Sunday Beauty is put to sleep, and a fair coin decides whether she wakes on Monday only or on Monday and Tuesday with her memory erased, so she never knows which day it is or whether she has woken before. The Sleeping Beauty problem still splits Bayesians between 1/2 and 1/3, over what counts as evidence when you are the one being sampled.
item.content:encoded: On Sunday Beauty is put to sleep, and a fair coin decides whether she wakes on Monday only or on Monday and Tuesday with her memory erased, so she never knows which day it is or whether she has woken before. item.title: Word of the Day: aporia — Daily Learning

item.title: Statistics: Overfitting and the Bias–Variance Tradeoff — Daily Learning
item.description: Say a betting model tuned to every quirk of the last 100 games looks unbeatable on those games, yet predicts the next 20 worse than a simpler model. That gap is the bias–variance tradeoff, the balance between a model too stiff to catch real patterns and one too jumpy to ignore noise, judged on unseen data rather than zero error on the past.

item.title: Statistics: Shrinkage — Daily Learning
item.description: When you estimate many things at once, the wildest results are usually part luck, so shrinkage pulls each estimate partway toward the group average, and the noisier or smaller the sample, the stronger the pull. Say a quarterback completes 80% of his passes in his first two games, with a league average of, say, 65%: rather than betting on 80%, you would bet nearer 70%, which is the James–Stein…
item.content:encoded: When you estimate many things at once, the wildest results are usually part luck, so shrinkage pulls each estimate partway toward the group average, and the noisier or smaller the sample, the stronger the pull. Say a quarterback completes 80% of his passes in his first two games, with a league average of, say, 65%: rather than betting on 80%, you would bet nearer 70%, which is the James–Stein idea, a deliberately biased guess that usually lands closer to the truth over a full season.

item.title: Big Idea: The Mandela Effect — Daily Learning
item.description: Large groups of people share the same false memory, down to the same wrong detail. That happens because recall rebuilds a memory instead of replaying it, filling gaps with whatever feels familiar.

item.title: Statistics: Conjugate Priors — Daily Learning
item.description: A conjugate prior is chosen so that, after new data arrive, the posterior stays in the same family as the prior, turning updating into simple arithmetic instead of messy integration. Start with a Beta(2, 2) prior for a coin's heads probability, roughly as if you had already seen about 2 heads and 2 tails worth of evidence, then observe 7 heads and 3 tails and just add the counts to get Beta(9,…
item.content:encoded: A conjugate prior is chosen so that, after new data arrive, the posterior stays in the same family as the prior, turning updating into simple arithmetic instead of messy integration. Start with a Beta(2, 2) prior for a coin's heads probability, roughly as if you had already seen about 2 heads and 2 tails worth of evidence, then observe 7 heads and 3 tails and just add the counts to get Beta(9, 5), a result that can become the next prior for a win-rate or conversion-rate estimate in sports betting or A/B testing.
